body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Engagement with a smartphone seizure diary and self-reported seizure control: a 12-month observational study","authors":"Mahlaba-Frost E, Kuznetsov-Adeyemi R, Lindgren-Obi T","year":2020,"venue":"Seizure Care Research","doi":"10.5555/scr.2020.0341","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 486 adults with epilepsy who installed a seizure diary app recommended by their clinic. Engagement was defined as at least one diary entry per week. At one month, 61 percent were engaged; at six months, 23 percent; at twelve months, 14 percent. Sustained users reported fewer missed doses, but they were also older, more often employed and had fewer seizures at baseline. Diary entries matched clinic-recorded seizures for 70 percent of sustained users. The authors caution that engagement and seizure control may share causes rather than one driving the other."},{"title":"How engagement is measured in self-management apps for chronic neurological conditions: a methodological review","authors":"Osei-Lambert A, Fujimoto-Hale C","year":2022,"venue":"Digital Neurology Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 61 studies of self-management apps for epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, migraine and Parkinson disease to see how engagement was defined. We found 23 different engagement measures. Log-ins and days of use were the most common, used in 38 studies; only 9 studies measured use of specific features, and 5 used a validated self-report engagement scale. Nineteen studies did not define engagement at all. Follow-up for engagement rarely exceeded three months. The authors propose reporting both use of core features and duration of use."},{"title":"Medication reminder use and antiseizure medication adherence measured by electronic pill boxes","authors":"Carvalho-Nyambura J, Stewart-Ikeda M, Brenner-Oduya K","year":2018,"venue":"Seizure Care Research","doi":"10.5555/scr.2018.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared app reminder logs with electronic pill box openings for 142 adults taking antiseizure medication over 90 days. Participants who acknowledged at least 80 percent of reminders had pill box adherence of 92 percent, compared with 78 percent for those who acknowledged fewer. Reminder use declined steadily over the 90 days. Participants who set their own reminder times acknowledged more reminders than those who used default times. The study did not measure seizures or quality of life, and participants were volunteers from one clinic."},{"title":"Why adults with epilepsy stop using self-management apps: a thematic analysis of 30 accounts","authors":"Ndlovu-Parris H, Aaltonen-Mensah S","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Digital Self-Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed written and spoken accounts from 30 adults with epilepsy who had stopped using a self-management app. Reasons included the effort of daily entries, apps that did not fit irregular seizure patterns, worry about who could see the data, and a lack of response from clinicians to the reports. Several participants said they would have kept using the app if a nurse had looked at their entries at clinic. People with memory problems after seizures found reminders helpful but diaries hard to complete."},{"title":"Digital access and app uptake among people with epilepsy in rural and low-income areas","authors":"Quispe-Harrington L, Bakshi-Wolde D, Thornton-Achebe M","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Digital Health Equity","doi":"10.5555/jdhe.2023.0129","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 1,020 adults attending four epilepsy clinics, 81 percent owned a smartphone, but ownership was 58 percent among those aged over 65 and 64 percent among those in the lowest income quintile. Of smartphone owners offered a self-management app, 47 percent installed it; installation was lower among people with intellectual disability and people who shared a phone. Limited mobile data was the reason most often given for not installing. The authors recommend that engagement studies report who was offered an app, not only who used it."},{"title":"Retention curves for health apps: an analysis of 1.2 million installs","authors":"Everett-Nakashima P, Diallo-Svensson G","year":2017,"venue":"Mobile Health Analytics","providerType":"report","abstract":"Using anonymous usage data from 1.2 million installs of 94 health apps, we estimated retention over 90 days. Seventy percent of users stopped opening an app within 30 days, and 88 percent within 90 days. Apps with reminders and clinician-linked features retained users longer, but retention also varied with the condition and the age of users. Usage data could not show whether people who stopped had benefited. The analysis did not include apps for epilepsy specifically, and app developers chose which data to share."},{"title":"Self-management programmes for epilepsy delivered digitally: a review of trials","authors":"Richter-Okeke B, Salazar-Whitfield N","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Neurology Reviews","doi":"10.5555/cnr.2024.0266","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified nine trials of digitally delivered self-management programmes for adults with epilepsy, with 1,340 participants. Programmes improved self-management scores modestly at three to six months. No trial showed a difference in seizure frequency, and only two reported engagement in enough detail to relate it to outcomes. Most trials excluded people with intellectual disability, and none reported outcomes by age or income. Follow-up beyond six months was reported by one trial only. The authors conclude that engagement is the missing link between digital programmes and outcomes."}]}
